dso.name: Andromeda Galaxy
facts: The most distant object most people can see with the naked eye — its light left 2.5 million years ago.
On a collision course with the Milky Way; the merger is expected in about 4.5 billion years.
Spans about six full moons of sky, but only its bright core is visible unaided.

dso.name: Orion Nebula
facts: The brightest nebula in the night sky — a fuzzy patch in Orion's sword, even with the naked eye.
A stellar nursery containing roughly 700 stars in the making.
The four hot young stars at its heart are called the Trapezium.

dso.name: Pleiades
facts: Also called the Seven Sisters; visible from every inhabited continent.
The Japanese car maker Subaru is named after this cluster — its logo shows six stars.
Hot blue young stars wrapped in wispy reflection nebulosity.

dso.name: Great Hercules Cluster
facts: About 300,000 stars packed into a ball only 145 light-years across.
Target of the 1974 Arecibo message, humanity's first deliberate radio broadcast to the stars.
The finest globular cluster visible from northern latitudes.

dso.name: Lagoon Nebula
facts: Visible from dark sites as a pale patch above the Teapot of Sagittarius.
Contains the Hourglass region, lit by two ferociously hot stars.
Dark dust columns cradle stars still being born.

dso.name: Ring Nebula
facts: A dying sun-like star shedding its outer layers into a glowing ring.
The white dwarf at its center burns at about 100,000 K.
Will fade away over the next few thousand years.

dso.name: Dumbbell Nebula
facts: One of the brightest planetary nebulae — a preview of the Sun's far future.
Its hourglass shape comes from gas escaping along two opposite directions.
Discovered by Charles Messier in 1764.

dso.name: Sombrero Galaxy
facts: Famous for its crisp edge-on dust lane, like a hat's brim.
Holds a supermassive black hole of roughly a billion solar masses.
Bright enough for small telescopes under dark skies.

dso.name: Whirlpool Galaxy
facts: The textbook grand-design spiral, printed in nearly every astronomy book.
Its small companion galaxy is gravitationally warping its arms.
The first galaxy recognized as a spiral, in 1845.

dso.name: Omega Nebula
facts: Also called the Swan Nebula for its graceful shape in telescopes.
One of the youngest star-forming regions known — about a million years old.
An easy binocular target from dark sites.

dso.name: Trifid Nebula
facts: Three-lobed — dark dust lanes split it visibly in small telescopes.
Combines three nebula types in one object: emission, reflection, and dark.
Spans about 40 light-years.

dso.name: Globular Cluster M4
facts: The nearest globular cluster to Earth.
Contains a famous millisecond pulsar with a planet orbiting it.
A distinctive bar of red giants streaks across its core.

dso.name: Butterfly Cluster
facts: Its brightest star glows orange among about 80 blue-white members.
Shaped like a butterfly through a telescope.
Apparent size about that of the full Moon.

dso.name: Ptolemy Cluster
facts: Recorded by Ptolemy in 130 AD — the oldest documented deep-sky object on this chart.
A naked-eye cluster of about 100 young stars.
A favorite binocular target in Scorpius.

dso.name: Wild Duck Cluster
facts: One of the richest, most compact open clusters — resembling a globular at low power.
Roughly 250 million years old.
Named by Admiral Smyth for its V shape of ducks in flight.

dso.name: Globular Cluster M22
facts: One of the brightest globulars — visible to the naked eye from dark southern sites.
Contains over 70,000 stars.
Fully resolves into individual points of light in telescopes.

dso.name: Triangulum Galaxy
facts: Third-largest member of our Local Group.
Under very dark skies, one of the farthest naked-eye objects you can spot.
Smaller and dimmer than Andromeda but more face-on.

dso.name: Crab Nebula
facts: The remnant of a supernova seen from Earth in 1054 AD, recorded by Chinese astronomers.
Contains a pulsar spinning 30 times per second.
The supernova was bright enough to see in daylight for 23 days.

dso.name: Beehive Cluster
facts: Known since antiquity; Hipparchus called it the Little Cloud.
Also called Praesepe — 'the manger'.
About 600 million years old, the same age as the Hyades.

dso.name: Bode's Galaxy
facts: One of the brightest galaxies in the northern sky, paired with the Cigar Galaxy.
A grand-design spiral visible in binoculars from dark skies.
Holds a central black hole of about 70 million solar masses.

dso.name: Cigar Galaxy
facts: A starburst galaxy, forming stars at ten times the Milky Way's rate.
Gravitational tugs from Bode's Galaxy funnel gas into its core, fueling the burst.
A supernova appeared here in 2014 — the closest in decades.

dso.name: Double Cluster
facts: Two young clusters side by side in Perseus — unmistakable in binoculars.
Only about 13 million years old; its stars are still massive and blue.
Catalogued by Hipparchus around 130 BC.

dso.name: Omega Centauri
facts: The largest globular orbiting the Milky Way — about 10 million stars.
Possibly the stripped core of a dwarf galaxy the Milky Way devoured long ago.
Unusually for a globular, it holds several generations of stars.

dso.name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
facts: A vast patch of the Milky Way's disk visible to the naked eye as a glowing cloud.
Your gaze here passes through a gap in dark dust lanes — a window into the galaxy.
Contains an estimated half a million stars in the telescopic field.

dso.name: Eagle Nebula
facts: Home of the Pillars of Creation, made famous by the Hubble Space Telescope.
Young massive stars are carving cavities out of dense molecular gas.
Spans about 70 by 55 light-years.

dso.name: North America Nebula
facts: Faintly visible to the naked eye from dark sites — just off Deneb in Cygnus.
Its shape resembles the continent; the 'Gulf of Mexico' is a dark dust lane.
Lit mostly by the ultraviolet glow of nearby Deneb.

dso.name: Coalsack Nebula
facts: A famous dark nebula beside the Southern Cross — a patch of sky with no stars.
Cold dust blocks the light of the Milky Way behind it.
Known to Aboriginal Australian peoples for tens of thousands of years.
